provenance: One text encoder or VAE sits inside dozens of unrelated bundles, so a content-hash lookup on a community site returns whichever bundle somebody uploaded first, and that stranger's permission flags then decide the licence of a file they did not publish. Each entry here is a file whose sha256 was traced back to the repository that actually publishes it, together with the licence tag that repository declares. Entries are added one misjudged case at a time; a mirror, a re-upload or a guess is not a source.

components.provenance: Checked 2026-10-11. sha256 equals the lfs.oid Hugging Face gives for model.safetensors at revision 999e0328 (size 603049496). The Hugging Face card says apache-2.0, but GET /api/organizations/CIDAS/members lists one member, nielsr, who converted the model into transformers; the organisation has no verification badge and every commit in the repository is his or the conversion bot's, so the tag was not set by the author. The author's own repository github.com/timojl/clipseg says in its README (master) 'The MIT license does not apply to these weights.' and 'The source code files in this repository (excluding model weights) are released under MIT license.'; in issue 35 'License of model weights' the author timojl answered on 2023-06-07 'There is no license specified for the weights. We released them for research purposes.' This row exists because files in a Hugging Face cache are now judged by the repository they belong to: without it the apache-2.0 tag would release these weights. spdx is 'none' on purpose - it is not on the allow-list, so a client that predates the verdict field reads this row as releasing nothing. The pinned address is kept so a recipient is told where to fetch the file.

The Hugging Face API for wangfuyun/AnimateLCM returns no licence in cardData and no licence tag, and the model card (main, read 2026-10-11) contains no licence statement. The code repository github.com/G-U-N/AnimateLCM carries an MIT licence; its README does not say that licence covers the released weights. With nothing stated for the weights the default answer applies. Without this row a content-hash lookup on Civitai finds a re-upload whose permission flags allow passing it on, and the file is released on a stranger's say-so. spdx is not on the allow-list on purpose, so a client that predates the verdict field reads this row as releasing nothing. The pinned address is kept so a recipient is told where to fetch the file.

components_note: A row releases a file only when it has sha256, origin_url and spdx, its origin is an authority the reader in licensing.py recognises and its licence is one we already pass on, so adding a releasing row cannot widen either of those; an empty table releases nothing and every file keeps the deny-by-default answer. A row with "verdict": "restricted" does the opposite: it marks a file we looked into and must not pass on, it wins over every releasing row for the same sha256 and over the licence tag of the repository the file sits in, and its "reason" is the sentence shown to the person packing. Such a row still carries origin_url (where a recipient fetches the file) and an spdx that is not on the allow-list. Entries arrive through the signed rules channel, which is the whole point of putting them here rather than in code - a shared part judged wrongly is fixed for everyone without a release.
